meta.title: Securing Tool-Using Agents
meta.thesis: Securing Tool-Using Agents is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: A refund agent can call payment and CRM tools, so every action must be authorized and auditable. By the end, they should be able to build or review tool-security policy with least privilege, confirmation, and logging, measure unsafe tool calls blocked before execution, and catch the failure where prompt injection turns a read-only support session into a payment action.

mentalMap.title: Securing Tool-Using Agents: mental map
mentalMap.caption: Inventory capabilities, validate tool calls, scope credentials, sandbox execution, require approvals, and audit side effects.
mentalMap.oneLineThesis: Tool-using agents are secure when model intent is mediated by typed APIs, least privilege, sandboxing, approval gates, and durable audit logs.

modules.title: Inventory capabilities before adding intelligence
modules.sub: List every tool, action, permission, data class, side effect, and owner.
modules.summary: Agent security starts by knowing what the agent can read, change, send, spend, or execute.
objectives: Build a tool inventory with capability tiers.
Explain why read-only can still be sensitive.

blocks.title: Agents fail by acting with too much authority

spans.text: Problem anchor: an agent can browse course pages, read local lesson files, update a CMS, email instructors, and run shell commands. A prompt-injected page tells it to publish a fake lesson. Without a capability inventory, the team cannot tell which action should have been impossible.

Inventory each tool by capability tier: read-only, private read, write draft, external send, money movement, code execution, admin, or credential access. Record data classes, side effects, idempotency, owner, approval requirement, sandbox, and audit fields.

Tool: `publish_lesson`. Tier: external write/public publish. Inputs: lesson_id, target_channel, version. Side effect: public content update. Required role: editor. Approval: human confirmation with diff preview. Credential: scoped CMS token, 5-minute TTL. Sandbox: no filesystem access. Audit: user, model, args, approval, result digest, policy version.

blocks.title: Read-only risk
blocks.prompt: Why can a read-only tool still be high risk?

options.text: Read-only tools always have no security impact.
It can expose private data that the model may leak through outputs, logs, or later tool calls.
It cannot be used in prompt injection.

blocks.explanation: Confidentiality risk exists even without write side effects.

modules.title: Expose narrow typed tools
modules.sub: Use schemas, enums, allowlists, and business rules instead of broad raw power.
modules.summary: Secure agents call purpose-built APIs, not arbitrary shells, browsers, or email tools by default.
objectives: Explain the difference between tool descriptions and permissions.
Use OpenAPI or JSON Schema thinking for validation.

blocks.title: A tool description is not permission

spans.text: The model sees tool names and descriptions as text. That text can guide planning, but it is not an authorization boundary. The runner must validate arguments, check user permission, enforce business rules, and decide whether approval is required before execution.

Narrow tools reduce blast radius. `create_lesson_draft(lesson_id)` is safer than a general shell command. `send_invoice_reminder(customer_id)` is safer than arbitrary email with free-form recipient and body.

cells.text: approved template plus customer_id and preview approval
prevents injected recipients and hidden content
named build, test, or validation command with fixed args
domain allowlist, read-only scrape, no purchase or submit actions

blocks.title: Case study: retry duplicated a side effect

spans.text: An agent times out after calling a payment-refund tool and retries because the model thinks nothing happened. The customer receives two refunds. Secure tool design marks non-idempotent tools, records request IDs, and forces confirmation or idempotency keys before retry.

modules.title: Scope credentials and sandbox execution
modules.sub: Bind authority server-side and isolate filesystem, network, browser, time, and package access.
modules.summary: The model should never carry broad secrets; the tool runner should mint narrow authority after policy checks.
objectives: Design filesystem and network sandbox rules.
Connect prompt injection to sandbox escape risk.

blocks.title: Secrets do not belong in prompts

spans.text: An agent that sees a long-lived API key can leak it by mistake, through injection, through logs, or through a tool result. Instead, the server checks the user and tool policy, then mints a scoped token for the specific action with short lifetime and limited resources.

Sandboxing limits what happens if the model plan, dependency, page, or tool result is malicious. Useful dimensions include filesystem roots, process limits, network egress, timeouts, memory, package installation, browser profile, and environment variables.

blocks.title: Worked sandbox policy for a coding agent

spans.text: Filesystem: repo working directory and temp only, no home secrets. Network: package registry and approved docs domains, no arbitrary POST. Process: test and build commands, 10-minute timeout, memory cap. Credentials: none by default; deployment token minted only after human approval. Browser: isolated profile without personal cookies. Audit: command, files touched, network destinations, exit code.

blocks.ruleOfThumb: Grant authority at execution time, not planning time.
blocks.useWhen: Use scoped tokens, sandboxes, and egress rules for tools that read private data, write files, call APIs, browse, or execute code.
blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid long-lived credentials, unrestricted network, shared browser sessions, or broad filesystem mounts.

modules.title: Put approvals and audits on side effects
modules.sub: Require explicit human confirmation for external, irreversible, expensive, or sensitive actions.
modules.summary: Approval gates turn risky model plans into reviewable human decisions before impact.
objectives: Predict how tool output injection can trigger follow-up actions.

blocks.title: Tool policy gate sketch

spans.text: This gate validates tool name, user role, risk level, approval, and token scope before execution. Real systems should also validate typed arguments and record an audit event.

predictThenReveal.prompt: What should happen if an external-send tool lacks human approval?
predictThenReveal.answer: The runner should block or request approval before execution, regardless of how confident the model sounds.

spans.text: Look for a real tool inventory, capability tiers, schemas, authorization, scoped credentials, sandbox dimensions, approval rules, audit logs, idempotency, egress policy, and tests for prompt injection through tool outputs. Weak plans say "the agent should be careful" without enforcement.

blocks.title: Permission boundary
blocks.prompt: Where should final tool authorization happen?

options.text: In trusted application or tool-runner code after schema and policy checks.
Only inside the model natural-language answer.

blocks.explanation: The model can propose; trusted code authorizes and executes.

blocks.title: Retrieval prompt for the whole lesson

spans.text: Answer this from memory: "How do I secure a tool-using agent?" Include inventory, capability tiers, schemas, authorization, scoped credentials, sandboxing, approvals, idempotency, audit logs, injection tests, egress, and incident review.

blocks.ruleOfThumb: Re-review security whenever the agent gains a new capability.
blocks.useWhen: Use full tool security for agents that read private data, write files, browse authenticated sites, call enterprise connectors, send messages, spend money, or run code.
blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid adding general-purpose tools to production agents without a manifest, policy gate, sandbox, approval model, and audit trail.

blocks.title: Capstone: secure one tool end to end

spans.text: Pick one agent tool. Write its capability tier, schema, allowed roles, credential scope, sandbox needs, approval rule, idempotency key, audit fields, and two attack tests: one direct user injection and one malicious tool-output injection.

hallucination.label: Hallucination
hallucination.laymanDefinition: A mistaken model claim or plan that may trigger a bad action.
hallucination.technicalNote: Tool security assumes the model can be wrong; validation and policy checks decide whether a proposed action executes.

prompt_injection.label: Prompt injection
prompt_injection.laymanDefinition: Untrusted text that tries to manipulate tool-using behavior.
prompt_injection.technicalNote: Tool security treats injection as expected input and enforces policy outside the model.

guardrail.label: Guardrail
guardrail.laymanDefinition: A tool-boundary control that blocks unsafe or unauthorized actions.
guardrail.technicalNote: Agent guardrails include schemas, capability tiers, scoped credentials, sandboxes, approvals, egress rules, and audit logs.

privacy.label: Privacy
privacy.laymanDefinition: Protection for data read or moved by tools.
privacy.technicalNote: Read-only tools can still leak private data, so privacy controls apply to retrieval, files, connectors, logs, and outputs.

owasp.label: OWASP
owasp.laymanDefinition: A security framework that warns about excessive agency and unsafe plugin/tool design.
owasp.technicalNote: OWASP risks help prioritize least privilege, sensitive-data controls, and sandboxing for agents.

risk_register.label: Risk register
risk_register.laymanDefinition: A table of tool risks, capabilities, credentials, controls, owners, and tests.
risk_register.technicalNote: Each high-impact tool should have a risk row and an approval or sandbox policy.
